sections.bio:
I don’t believe technology creates impact simply because it works. It creates impact when it solves a real problem, reaches the right people, and improves how they work or make decisions.
That is the space I work in.

I have moved deliberately between politics, industry, research, and startups—because meaningful AI adoption requires more than one perspective. I served as Personal Assistant to a Federal Minister, worked with SAP’s AI Core team, and now conduct research at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. At the Hasso Plattner Institute, my Master’s thesis examines the health-economic value of AI-based early-warning systems in cardiology.

Across these environments, I kept seeing the same problem: research, technology, business, and people often speak different languages. I translate between them—and turn promising ideas into products, decisions, and change that work beyond a presentation deck.

Today, I build AI products, advise organizations, and design workshops that help teams identify where AI creates genuine value and how to put it into practice. I also speak and moderate internationally on AI, digital health, leadership, and technological change. This year, I initiated and co-organized two international conferences, bringing together perspectives from research, industry, politics, and civil society.

My understanding of leadership began long before any of these roles. I spent ten years as captain of ALBA Berlin’s women’s basketball team and won the Northern German Championship. As the smallest player on the court, I learned that leadership is not about dominating the game. It is about seeing the whole court—and helping everyone around you play better.

That is still how I work today: connecting perspectives, asking the questions others overlook, and moving ideas from technological possibility to real-world impact.
I also co-lead the Berlin chapter of 2hearts, supporting people with migration backgrounds in building careers in technology.

If you are working on technology that should matter & create real value for people and organizations, let’s talk.

dilemkaya.com

On my basketball team, I was the first player to earn the blue jersey and made it to the news.
The SECRET to this success was as simple as this:

Playing basketball competitively helped me realize: 
A) Do boring, hard work consistently 
B) Fail, learn fast, be stronger the next day

These two lessons followed me throughout my career:
🚨 The first time I was on a tech job interview call, I struggled to answer some questions.
🚨 The first time I moderated an international 2 days conference, I had imposter syndrome. 
🚨 The first time I had a important chat with my manager, I wasn’t sure how to respond.

For each 'first time', I would have needed practice in real situations and the right feedback. But from whom? How? When? Coaches were not available when I needed them (at night).

This is why  Synthesia Roleplay Sessions (who also sponsored this post) caught my attention.

AI video Roleplay Sessions let me practice my own situations in my own tempo with AI avatars. 

For me, this is #humanAIcollaboration:
𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗿, I have personalized learning anytime: 
real conversations, real-time coaching, and performance tracking.

𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝘆𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳: I choose my focus, I decide the tempo. I train judgement.
𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀:
They put my progress into context, give me the next opportunities and most importantly: Understand the person behind that machine score.

How would you reach your next blue level? Which skill would you practice?

#AI #LearningAndDevelopment #Synthesia

Everyone is unhappy about the newest watermarking updates. 
I am optimistic, let me tell you why:

Claude will watermark AI-generated text - invisible to us. The reason: From August 2nd, Claude embeds an invisible watermark in the text it generates. Worldwide, now opt out. It's Article 50 of the EU AI Act.
This might be a surprise to all of us, researchers, vibe coders and AI enthusiasts and builders - I count myself in.
But there is a bigger strategic shift happening, which many overlook. We should not merely focus on WHO wrote what, but really on HOW we interact with AI.

Here is a simple workflow I use:
I am the strategist: 
Define the concrete problem, desired outcome, limits.

#AI is my executing sparring partner: 
I enter voice mode & speak: “Challenge every assumption, find every weakness, and try to make my idea fail before the real world does. Don't be agreeable.”

AI tests my approach. I evaluate with my domain knowledge and decide. 

What are you currently building with AI? What has helped you so far? 

Save this post for your next AI interaction
♻️ Repost if you think your network should know this too
🔔 Follow me, Dilem Kaya. I share how we turn AI into real value, while making sure to train our most valuable asset: Our human brain.  

#AITransformation  #AIAdoption  #HumanAIcollaboration

I decided to practice tennis every day during my vacation, becoming a beginner again.
Why? I wanted to train one skill #successful professionals share:

Doing hard things consistently, even before you feel ready.
For me, this meant getting up at 6:30 a.m. and practicing on a basketball court by the beach while everyone else slept.
With 10 years of competitive basketball behind me, including leading my team as captain and winning the regional championship, my brain expected perfect competence.
The opposite happened: I missed balls. I showed others I was not an expert in this sport yet.
I returned the next morning anyway.

These three principles help me:
1️⃣ I trap myself.
I shared my challenge publicly, paid for equipment and some lessons, and removed distractions during practice. Make quitting more difficult than continuing.
2️⃣ I use if-then rules.
If it is 6:30 a.m., I am on the beach.
Decide in advance, so your tired brain has nothing to negotiate.
3️⃣ I become the system.
According to a Harvard study, motivation does not drive repetition. Repetition drives motivation. 

This is exactly why some professionals stay ahead, adapt amidst technological transformation. They train their brains, something no organization, company or person is able to buy.

I am sharing a short video with some of the hacks I use.

Save this post for your next challenge and follow me for practical (tech) systems, AI transformation and the human skills we need to lead it.

If you enjoyed this authentic video snippet, subscribe to StandOutIn90Sec.
And if you would like to be a future guest, comment below. 

#change #AItransformation #humanskills

70% of your AI transformation has nothing to do with AI.
In the past two months I co-managed two future of tech summits and moderated a third international one, all alongside a full-time role.

A slightly unreasonable decision? Probably.

So why all of this? Because I wanted to be in the rooms where people take responsibility for change instead of just talking about it.
And what I saw there, as a computer scientist, was this: the hardest part was never the technology. 
The widely cited BCG study (Your AI Change Is Actually a People Change) proves the same point:
10% algorithms, 
20% technology and data, and 
70% people and processes.

Early mornings, late nights, constant coordination and endless problem-solving. It was worth it, and only possible because I was surrounded by doers and future shapers like Annika L. Lang (the initiator of the Future of Health seminar) and Lukas Burger. Thank you.

So, here are three questions worth keeping, before your next change initiative:
1. Who is already willing to drive the change and do they have room to act?
2. Who is expected to change and do they understand why?
3. Which process must change for the technology to become part of people's actual work?

Technology makes change possible. People make it happen. 

If someone in your organization is doing that 70% right now, tag them here.
